claims.text: The starting alloy is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced by conventional powder processing.
The proposed intervention is addition of 0.5 vol% Y2O3 nanoparticles during mechanical alloying followed by consolidation such as spark plasma sintering.
The processing route will produce a uniform Y2O3 nanoparticle dispersion in the alloy.
The Y2O3 nanoprecipitates will be thermally stable.
The Y2O3 nanoprecipitates will decorate grain boundaries and also reside within grains.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as sinks for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will pin grain boundaries.
Defect trapping and grain-boundary pinning will reduce the solute diffusion responsible for radiation-induced precipitation.
Grain-boundary pinning will prevent grain coarsening and preserve the nanocrystalline structure.
At approximately 8 dpa, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have 50–70% less radiation-induced precipitate volume fraction than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have a lower density of irradiation-induced defects than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening or exhibit less hardening than the unmodified alloy.
Adding Y2O3 will enhance sinterability and improve bulk processing characteristics.
The predicted benefits apply around 8 dpa at irradiation temperatures of 400–500°C and after post-irradiation treatments up to 600°C.
The benefits depend on avoiding significant Y2O3 nanoparticle coarsening or agglomeration.
Y2O3 nanoparticle coarsening could reduce point-defect absorption efficiency.
